title: UNITARES: Information-Theoretic Governance of Heterogeneous Agent Fleets
researchTitle: UNITARES: Information-Theoretic Governance of Heterogeneous Agent Fleets
author: Kenny Wang
summary: The system itself: how UNITARES tracks the working state of very different kinds of agents, judging each against its own kind rather than one standard for the whole fleet.
abstract: UNITARES is a runtime governance framework for heterogeneous fleets of AI agents. Each agent carries a four-dimensional state estimate updated at each check-in to support longitudinal state tracking and policy actions across processes that do not share an output modality, a tempo, or a healthy operating point.

The paper specifies the four-dimensional coordinate definitions, a class-conditional calibration protocol that normalizes each agent against its own class rather than a single fleet-wide distribution, a continuous-time contraction analysis, and a pipeline-ordering migration mechanism for introducing re-grounded state estimates without disrupting live policy decisions. Dated deployment measurements, calibration analyses, and scope boundaries are reported in the full text.

title: Trajectory Identity: A Mathematical Framework for Enactive AI Self-Hood
researchTitle: Trajectory Identity: A Mathematical Framework for Enactive AI Self-Hood
author: Kenny Wang
summary: Proposes that an agent's identity is the pattern its behavior keeps over time, where it tends to settle and how it recovers, rather than an ID or a store of memories.
abstract: Conventional approaches to AI agent identity rely on static identifiers such as UUIDs and session tokens or on accumulated memory stores. This paper proposes a mathematical framework grounded in dynamical systems theory that treats identity as a behavioral trajectory over time rather than a stored label.

The framework defines a trajectory signature computed from longitudinal time-series observations — homeostatic state distributions, preference formation, self-model calibration, and perturbation recovery dynamics — to study within-agent continuity across sessions, semantics for agent forking and merging, and the conditions under which behavioral signatures can or cannot discriminate individual agents across harnesses and operating regimes.

title: A Flat Coherence Score: What a Production-Data Replay Does and Does Not Show About Agent Self-State Gating
researchTitle: A Flat Coherence Score: What a Production-Data Replay Does and Does Not Show About Agent Self-State Gating
author: Kenny Wang
summary: Examines whether the deployed coherence score could actually decide anything at its own thresholds, and what replacing it with a score measured against each class of agent does and does not show.
abstract: A running multi-agent governance system computes a scalar coherence score at each agent check-in and uses it, among other inputs, to assign each state to a high, boundary, or low operating basin. This paper audits how that deployed score behaved against its own decision thresholds on frozen operational windows.

Through a reproducible offline counterfactual replay, the study compares the legacy scalar against a class-conditional replacement measured relative to each agent class's operating point, separating what a label-change replay establishes about threshold sensitivity from open questions of label validity, drift across observation windows, and downstream outcome prediction.

title: Accountability Without a Trusted Center: A Federated Governance Testbed for Multi-Principal AI Agents
author: Kenny Wang
summary: Designs an open testbed for holding agents accountable across organizations that do not trust each other, pre-registers how it will be evaluated, and runs its attestation mechanism between two machines.
abstract: AI agents increasingly delegate, persist, clone, and act across shared infrastructure for principals who do not trust one another and share no central controller. The accountability questions in that setting are relational — which process acted, who authorized it, and through what delegation chain — and controls that assume a single privileged operator cannot answer them by construction.

This paper presents the design and pre-registered evaluation plan for an open testbed in which each principal runs its own governance instance and cross-principal interactions are mediated by cryptographic attestations rather than a trusted center, alongside a two-host verification run exercising the attestation object's refusal conditions across an offline boundary.

title: Signed Is Not True: Measuring What Provenance Checks Catch in an LLM Agent Handoff
researchTitle: Signed Is Not True: Measuring What Provenance Checks Catch in an LLM Agent Handoff
author: Kenny Wang
summary: Measures what cryptographic origin checks and evidence comparisons catch — and how verification badges and instructions change receiver decisions — across a two-principal agent handoff with database ground truth. Run November 2026.
abstract: Handoffs between AI agents across organizational boundaries are increasingly secured by proving origin through cryptographic signatures, verifiable agent identifiers, and signed mandates. A signature answers who sent a message, whereas the receiving principal's operational question is whether the reported work actually occurred.

This study evaluates rule-based verification gates and LLM receivers in a two-principal refund and payout pipeline backed by database ground truth, comparing origin-only checks, state-digest evidence checks, verification badges, and receiver instructions across planted false reports and organic tool-failure handoffs.

title: When Structured Disagreement Backfires: Pre-Registered Evaluation of Crux Briefs vs. Common-Ground Summaries Under Saturated Advisory Panels
researchTitle: When Structured Disagreement Backfires: Crux Briefs vs. Common-Ground Summaries
author: Kenny Wang
summary: Pre-registered, blinded benchmark comparing structured two-sided disagreement cards against common-ground summaries, single advisors, and unbriefed decisions across paired flawed and sound decision packets. Run November 2026.
abstract: Decision makers reviewing consequential packets with an AI assistant face paired hazards of uncritical deferral on flawed inputs and false alarms on sound ones. Multi-model advisory tools can either synthesize common ground or preserve structured two-sided cruxes where advisors disagree.

This study evaluates a local multi-family briefing pipeline in a pre-registered, blinded benchmark of paired flawed and sound decision scenarios across four domains, comparing unbriefed decisions, single-advisor briefs, common-ground synthesis, and structured disagreement cards across cross-family synthesizer and decider pairings.

title: Execution-Attested Side-Effect Gating at the NLIP Type-3 Boundary
researchTitle: Execution-Attested Side-Effect Gating at the NLIP Type-3 Boundary
author: Kenny Wang
summary: Design and evaluation of a deterministic ECMA-430/ECMA-434 Type-3 Security Extension that gates side-effecting publication calls on snapshot-verified Git tree receipts. Run November 2026.
abstract: Open-source AI agents increasingly invoke side-effecting tools such as code publication and repository mutation across standardized communication layers like the Natural Language Interaction Protocol (NLIP, ECMA-430), where agent self-reports and post-check working-tree edits can bypass prompt-level instructions.

This report presents nlip-receipts, a deterministic Type-3 Security Extension for NLIP that permits publication if and only if an authorized caller references an immutable Git tree digest previously verified inside an isolated archive snapshot under the active policy epoch and destination profile, and maps the mechanism to ECMA-434 security countermeasures.
